papers.title: Direct tumour-adipocyte contact / Stroma AReactive Invasion Front Areas (TAC/SARIFA) in advanced oropharyngeal cancer
papers.abstract: Introduction: Stroma areactive invasion front areas (SARIFA) are a histopathological phenomenon at the tumour invasion front characterised by direct tumour-adipocyte contact (TAC). It can be detected on histological Haematoxylin-Eosin (H&E) stained tumour slides. TAC/SARIFA has emerged as a strong negative prognostic factor in several tumour entities. In this monocentric retrospective study, we aim to elucidate the impact of TAC/SARIFA in oropharyngeal cancer. Materials and methods: 78 cases of pT3 to pT4 oropharyngeal squamous cell cancer from 2005 to 2023 and their corresponding lymph nodes were analysed for the occurrence of TAC/SARIFA. Besides, we compared overall survival rates, recurrence-free survival (RFS) and association with biological and pathological tumour characteristics. Results: In total, overall survival was significantly reduced in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours (p=0.014). Moreover, TAC/SARIFA positive primary tumours are associated with TAC/SARIFA positive lymph nodes (p<0.001) and extranodal extension (ENE) (p=0.032). Finally, RFS in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours was reduced, but not significantly (p=0.072). No significant difference was found between p16 positive and p16 negative tumours and prevalence of TAC/SARIFA. Conclusion: TAC/SARIFA is a possible prognostically relevant risk factor in oropharyngeal cancer. When detected in the primary tumour or lymph nodes, it is associated with reduced overall survival rates and tendency towards shorter RFS. TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes almost always show ENE.

papers.title: Aneuploidy and structural genome complexity beyond the EWSR1 fusion is associated with evolution and outcome in clear cell sarcoma
authors: L. S. P. D. S. Tavares
papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare cancer defined by EWSR1-CREB gene family fusions with clinical outcomes that range from indolent to chemotherapy-refractory metastatic disease. Through multi-omic profiling of primary, recurrent and metastatic tumours and cell lines, we show that CCS is more genomically complex than previously recognised. Beyond the fusion, tumours acquire chromoplexy, chromothripsis and an intermediate aneuploidy burden, with ongoing subclonal diversification. Recurrent events include chromosome17q gain and inactivation of the MYC antagonist MGA. Enriched transcriptional signatures of chromosomal instability,17q gain, 9p21.3 loss and TERT alteration each double the hazard of death, supporting a new molecular based CCS risk stratification framework at diagnosis. Transcriptomes converge on a MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis programme, a previously unrecognised therapeutic vulnerability. These findings address a central paradox of CCS, a shared oncogenic identity with divergent clinical fate, implicating tolerated aneuploidy and chromosomal diversification as candidate determinants of progression.

papers.title: Beyond standardized health-related quality of life measures: Additional symptoms and problems reported through the EORTC WISP instrument in the EUonQoL-Kit study across European cancer populations
papers.abstract: Background: Standardized health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures may not capture all symptoms/problems relevant to people with cancer. The European Oncology Quality of Life toolkit (EUonQoL-Kit), co-created with multiple stakeholders to inform health policy across Europe, combines standardized closed-ended patient-reported outcome (PRO) items with the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) open-ended Write In three Symptoms/Problems (WISP) instrument. We aimed to identify symptoms/problems reported via WISP beyond the EUonQoL-Kit, examine differences in background characteristics between WISP respondents and non-respondents, and compare additional symptom/problem reporting across three target cancer populations: patients in active treatment, survivors, and patients in palliative care. Methodology: This descriptive analysis used data from adults with current or previous cancer diagnoses participating in a multicenter validation study across 32 European countries (22 August 2024 - 7 July 2025). WISP responses were categorized, and subsequently their prevalence and severity were calculated. Participant characteristics and the ten most frequently reported additional symptoms/problems were compared across groups using t-tests, chi-square tests, or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. Results: Among 4,284 included participants, 519 (12.1%) reported 954 symptoms/problems on WISP, of which 383 (40.1%) were not covered by EUonQoL-Kit v2 closed-ended items. Women, participants from Western and Northern Europe, highly educated and those diagnosed with breast cancer were more likely to respond to the WISP than other subgroups (all p < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were found in the prevalence of common additional symptoms/problems (p [≥] 0.130). Descriptively, numbness/tingling, skin problems and bleeding were most reported by patients in active treatment; indigestion, incontinence, and vision problems in survivors; and edema, cough and itching in palliative care. Conclusions: The EORTC WISP complemented standardized PRO assessment by capturing additional symptoms/problems. Integrating open-ended WISP reporting into the final toolkit may enhance HRQoL assessment across European cancer populations while identifying population-specific concerns without expanding predefined items for all respondents.

papers.title: Spatial proteomics identifies a myeloid-dominated, compartmentalized microenvironment and a proliferation-associated prognostic signature in clear cell sarcoma
papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is a rare soft-tissue sarcoma with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Because of its rarity, the composition, spatial organization, and functional relevance of the CCS tumour microenvironment and tumour cell heterogeneity remain largely unexplored. Here, to address this gap, and as part of the Clear Cell Sarcoma Consortium, we used imaging mass cytometry with two antibody panels to generate a single-cell, spatially resolved proteomic map of CCS, profiling more than 5 million cells from a multi-institutional, clinically annotated formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded cohort of 52 patients. Our analysis shows that CCS is immune-cold, with the tumour centre dominated by myeloid cells, principally CD68+ and CD163+ macrophages, whereas the invasive front harbours a more diverse, lymphoid-containing immune infiltrate. Within the tumour compartment, we identified a proliferative tumour cell phenotype associated with shorter overall survival. Deep visual proteomics further identified a global proliferation signature enriched for cell-cycle and replication programmes in tumours with high abundance of this phenotype. Further, deep-learning-based models could predict the abundance of the proliferative tumour phenotype in haematoxylin-and-eosin images, which may suggest a path toward future patient stratification in the clinic. Finally, we identified c-MET and B7-H3 as candidate antibody-drug conjugate targets without significant regional or primary-metastasis differences in expression. Together, this work illuminates the spatial proteomic landscape of CCS and highlights candidate markers for patient stratification and potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: CB-COMIL: interpretable prediction of melanoma immunotherapyresponse from multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images
papers.abstract: Deep learning models can predict melanoma immunotherapy response but rarely explain predictions biologically. Concept bottleneck models offer interpretable predictions, but have not been applied to multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and whether their learned concepts reproduce tissue measurements remains unclear. We developed CB-COMIL, which routes mIF predictions through four supervised concepts (immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index), decomposing each prediction exactly into concept contributions. Developed on 211 slides and evaluated on 42 slides from an independent, differently acquired test cohort, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020, 95% CI: -0.103 to 0.144). In 41 slides with complete measurements, learned concepts correlated with measured counterparts (Spearman: 0.61; 0.61-0.76), yet substituting measured values reduced macro-F1 from 0.68 to 0.48. CB-COMIL makes predictions interpretable without detectable performance loss, and our evaluation shows that concepts can faithfully determine predictions without reproducing the corresponding biological measurements.

papers.title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors
papers.abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

papers.title: Panel-agnostic tumour-only diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency
papers.abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.

papers.title: CIRCULATING IMMUNE DYNAMICS DURING NEOADJUVANT CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY IN EARLY TRIPLE-NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER
papers.abstract: Background: Pathological complete response (pCR) after pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy predicts improved outcomes in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but circulating immune determinants of response remain poorly characterized. Methods: The study included 64 patients with early TNBC treated with pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Flow cytometry analyzed 125 peripheral-blood specimens collected at baseline, during treatment and before surgery. Baseline PBMCs from 22 patients underwent scRNA-seq, generating 135,271 quality-controlled cells. Analyses used nonparametric tests, effect sizes, FDR correction and sensitivity analyses. Results: Baseline scRNA-seq identified response-associated transcriptional differences. Patient-level pseudo-bulk analysis revealed enrichment of TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB signaling in cytotoxic T/NK and B cells from non-pCR patients (global q<=3.94e-7), together with MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling in cytotoxic T/NK cells (both global q=7.00e-5). T-cell analyses suggested preserved naive/memory features in pCR, while a higher proportion of CX3CR1-expressing cells within the CD4 memory/activation-like compartment was associated with pCR (q=0.0157; AUC=0.949). In B cells, pCR was associated with a nominally higher naive-like program score (P=0.029; q=0.059), supported by higher IGHM and IGHD signals, whereas XBP1 was higher in non-pCR. Flow cytometry identified treatment-associated B-cell remodeling. At pre-surgery, switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR than non-pCR patients (62.6% versus 50.0%; P=0.0086; q=0.0667; Cliff's delta=0.651; AUC=0.825) and remained nominally significant in leave-one-patient-out analyses. Early increases in unswitched-memory B-cell CD38 balance were numerically greater in non-pCR patients, whereas pre-surgery switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR patients. Conclusions: Baseline inflammatory and metabolic pathway enrichment was associated with non-pCR, whereas pCR-associated T-cell findings included a CD4 memory/activation-associated CX3CR1 signal and trends towards preserved naive/memory features. Together with time- and compartment-dependent B-cell remodeling, these findings nominate circulating transcriptional states and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics for prospective validation as candidate biomarkers of pathological response.

papers.title: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
papers.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

papers.title: Circulating miRNA profiling identifies hsa-miR-23a-3p and a three-miRNA signature associated with serous ovarian cancer
papers.abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most lethal subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for minimally invasive biomarkers that support disease detection and molecular characterization. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising candidates, although their clinical applicability remains limited by methodological variability and insufficient validation. Plasma samples from 100 individuals (50 patients with ovarian cancer and 50 cancer-free controls) were initially collected from four biobanks. Following quality control, 94 samples (47 patients and 47 controls) were included in the final analysis. Eight candidate miRNAs were quantified using RT-qPCR, and relative expression was assessed following global mean normalization. Differential expression was evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, while discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Three-miRNA logistic regression models were additionally explored using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Among the eight candidates, hsa-miR-23a-3p exhibited significantly lower circulating expression in patients with ovarian cancer than in controls (p = 2.14 x 10-5), achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.755 (95% CI, 0.657-0.852), with 93.6% sensitivity and 53.2% specificity at the selected threshold. Exploratory analysis across FIGO stages revealed heterogeneous expression patterns, although the limited number of early-stage cases precluded definitive conclusions regarding stage-specific performance. A three-miRNA signature comprising hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-21-5p, and hsa-miR-20a-5p achieved an apparent AUC of 0.798. However, repeated cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.716 {+/-} 0.022, indicating reduced performance after internal validation. Variability in exogenous spike-in Ct values and the marked imbalance in biobank representation between study groups highlighted potential pre-analytical confounding. Circulating hsa-miR-23a-3p showed moderate discriminatory performance between patients with ovarian cancer and cancer-free controls, supporting its further investigation as a candidate liquid biopsy biomarker. Although combining three miRNAs improved apparent classification performance, this advantage was not established through internal validation. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sample provenance, technical variability, and model overfitting when evaluating circulating miRNA signatures. Independent validation in appropriately balanced cohorts is required before clinical applicability can be established.

papers.title: # Treatment- and tissue-context-specific isotope labeling patterns in patient-derived lung cancer tissues: an independent reanalysis of public metabolomics data
papers.abstract: Publicly deposited stable-isotope-resolved metabolomics data can be reanalyzed independently, but small patient-derived experiments may produce treatment effects with limited statistical resolution. We reanalyzed a public isotope-resolved metabolomics dataset from patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures to quantify treatment- and tissue-specific labeling patterns and their uncertainty. We used 38 tissue samples from two patients: matched tumor and non-tumor slices from UK131 treated with vehicle or pembrolizumab and traced with U-13C6-glucose or U-13C5,15N2-glutamine (n = 3 per cell), and a pembrolizumab x WGP {beta}-glucan factorial experiment in UK2035 tumor tissue (n = 3/3/3/2). We recomputed protein-normalized pools, isotopologue distributions, atom-percent excess and pathway summaries. Effects were estimated with log2-scale linear models, Hedges' g, and exact randomization tests that enumerated all assignments compatible with each design; Benjamini-Hochberg q values were calculated within endpoint families. Sixteen macrophage samples were examined only descriptively. In UK131 tumor tissue, labeled non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates increased 1.84-fold (model P = 0.036; exact tumor P = 0.10; exact interaction P = 0.16; q = 0.32). Weighted isotopic scrambling increased 1.31-fold (exact interaction P = 0.04; q = 0.20), and glutamine-derived glutathione diversion increased 1.66-fold (exact interaction P = 0.09; q = 0.22). In UK2035, the combination increased the labeled IMP/(ATP+GTP+UTP) ratio 3.64-fold (model interaction P = 3.2 x 10-4; exact P = 0.016; q = 0.097). No endpoint survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 in the exact analyses. The reanalysis reproduced the direction of the source study's principal labeling patterns but showed that their statistical support is weaker than model-based P values imply. These results should be treated as hypothesis-generating estimates for larger patient-derived studies, not as evidence of a validated metabolic bottleneck.

papers.title: A pilot study of the mutational landscape of colorectal cancer in Black South Africans
papers.abstract: BackgroundColorectal cancer (CRC) is a public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where the molecular landscape of the disease remains poorly characterised. In particular, genomic studies of resident Black African populations are limited, and the contribution of population-specific mutational processes and potential infectious exposures remains insufficiently understood. The Molecular, Somatic and Infectious Drivers of Colorectal Cancer in Africa (MOSAIC) collaboration aims to address these gaps by generating population-specific genomic data. This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of paired tumour-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and to provide an initial characterisation of somatic mutations and mutational signatures in South African patients with CRC. MethodsWe recruited five Black South African patients with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive CRC through the CoRecT Cancer study at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital And Wits University Donald Gordon Medical Centre, Johannesburg. Fresh-frozen colorectal tumour tissue and matched peripheral blood samples were subjected to paired-end WGS (2 x 151 bp) using the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform. Somatic variants were identified using CaVEMan and Strelka2, followed by functional annotation using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP). Protein-altering variants were characterised using the R package maftools. Mutational signature contributions were estimated using SigProfilerAssignment and the COSMIC v3 reference catalogue. ResultsAll ten sequencing samples, comprising five tumour-blood pairs, passed quality control. Estimated sequencing depth ranged from 49.2X to 82.4X for tumour samples and from 22.7X to 40.7X for matched blood samples, with a median of 96.3% well-aligned reads. Following somatic variant calling and filtering, the number of retained mutations ranged from 1,106 to 65,379 per tumour. Three of the five tumours harboured at least one predicted protein-altering variant, comprising seven missense and four splice-site variants across eleven genes. Mutational signature analysis of single base substitutions (SBS) revealed inter-individual heterogeneity. SBS1 and SBS5 were detected across all five tumours, while additional signatures included SBS18, SBS20, SBS26 and SBS44, among others. Several tumours exhibited signatures associated with mismatch repair-related mutational processes. ConclusionsThis pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of paired tumour-normal WGS and preliminary somatic mutation profiling in Black South African patients with CRC. The findings provide initial insights into the heterogeneous mutational landscape of CRC in this underrepresented population. However, the small sample size and incomplete clinical and molecular characterisation necessitate cautious interpretation. Larger studies incorporating comprehensive mismatch repair assessment, copy-number and structural variant analysis, germline susceptibility profiling and investigation of infectious exposures will be essential to validate these preliminary observations and better understand the molecular and environmental drivers of CRC in African populations.

papers.title: TP53 and Co-Occurring Pathogenic Variants Are Differentially Associated with Prognosis of Advanced Ovarian and Endometrial Carcinomas
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo determine whether TP53 and other pathogenic variants (PVs) carry shared or organ-specific prognostic associations in advanced ovarian and endometrial carcinoma. MethodsWe analyzed 1060 patients with stage III-IV ovarian carcinoma (924 high-grade serous [HGSOC], 66 clear cell [CCOC], 42 endometrioid, 28 mucinous) and 543 with endometrial carcinoma (EC) profiled by next-generation sequencing. Associations with overall survival (OS) were estimated by multivariable Cox regression and combined across organs by fixed-effect pooling. Key findings were tested in 8881 tumors from public cBioPortal cohorts, including The Cancer Genome Atlas. ResultsTP53 PV was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23-2.10) and CCOC (HR 3.23, 1.05-9.89) but not in HGSOC overall (HR 0.95, 0.72-1.25); in HGSOC, it was associated with worse OS only in KRAS-mutant tumors (HR 3.42, 1.13-10.33). KRAS PV was associated with better OS in CCOC (HR 0.29, 0.09-0.89) and HGSOC (HR 0.72, 0.50-1.02) but not in EC. In HGSOC, BRCA1/2 PV was associated with better OS and MYC amplification with worse OS. In EC, CTNNB1 and ARID1A PVs were associated with better OS. RB1 PV was associated with worse OS in both organs (pooled HR 1.47, 1.05-2.06). In public cohorts stratified by histology, TP53 alteration was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.69, 1.36- 2.10) and ovarian carcinoma (HR 1.28, 1.00-1.62). ConclusionsThe prognostic association of TP53 PV depends on organ, histotype and co- occurring KRAS PV, and RB1 PV is a shared adverse marker. These findings may inform prognostic stratification of Mullerian carcinomas.

papers.title: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients ([~]55% vs [~]75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDMcA, C2CD2, TAF2, SLCcA1c, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIMc4B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

papers.title: Feasibility and Psychological Outcomes of a Clinical Meditation Intervention for Patients with Cancer: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPsychological care is an important component of cancer care, addressing psychological distress and supporting patients as they cope with illness. Meditation-based approaches, including mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have been incorporated into supportive cancer care internationally. Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho), a meditation method developed in Japan, integrates traditional Buddhist meditation with a contemporary medical care perspective. However, its feasibility and psychological outcomes in patients with cancer have not been sufficiently studied. ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Clinical Meditation intervention and to explore psychological outcomes and participants experiences among patients with cancer who were receiving or scheduled to receive pharmacotherapy at the time of recruitment. MethodsThis single-arm pilot study used a convergent mixed-methods design to evaluate an 8-week program consisting of a 4-week structured phase (1 face-to-face session and 3 brief online group sessions, with prescribed home practice) and a 4-week self-directed phase (1 individual online session, with voluntary home practice). Feasibility was assessed descriptively using retention, attendance, practice frequency, and poststudy feedback. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, fatigue, spiritual well-being (SWB), and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were assessed at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Changes were examined using Friedman tests and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Free-text responses were analyzed thematically and integrated with questionnaire findings at the participant level. ResultsEleven patients were enrolled; 9 (81.8%) completed the 4-week assessment and 8 (72.7%) completed the 8-week assessment. Median practice frequency declined from 5-6 days per week during the structured first month to 3-4 days per week during the self-directed second month (P=.031). Quantitative analyses included 9 participants, of whom 8 completed all 3 assessments; qualitative analyses included 8 participants. SWB and PTG showed significant overall changes (adjusted P=.02 and P=.04, respectively). SWB was higher than baseline at 4 weeks (adjusted P=.012), but the difference was not significant at 8 weeks. PTG was higher than baseline at both 4 and 8 weeks (both adjusted P=.047). No significant changes were observed in anxiety, depression, insomnia, or fatigue. Five themes were identified, encompassing experiences such as relaxation, greater distance from rumination, and meditation as a source of support. Participants accounts generally aligned with increases in SWB and PTG scores, although perceived benefits did not always correspond to changes in all questionnaire measures. ConclusionsThis mixed-methods pilot study suggests that Clinical Meditation may be feasible and acceptable for patients with cancer, although sustaining meditation practice remains challenging. Exploratory increases in SWB and PTG warrant further investigation. Larger controlled studies, comparisons with established MBIs, and deeper qualitative research are needed to evaluate outcomes and clarify the distinctive features of Clinical Meditation.

papers.title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
authors: Y. A. J. van de Wouw
H. J. G. van de Werken
papers.abstract: BackgroundCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. MethodsWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). ResultsHigh-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. ConclusionsCUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

papers.title: CONSORTiUM-IO: A Phase 1 Study Evaluating VE800 Plus Nivolumab in Treatment of Select Refractory or Metastatic Cancers
papers.abstract: Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCEThe first-in-human study of the safety and efficacy of a defined bacterial consortium in combination with anti-PD-1 treatment in various solid tumors demonstrated the safety of the combination, albeit with low clinical efficacy. The results provide important knowledge and considerations about microbiome modulation in cancer, to help design future trials.

papers.title: Phase I Clinical Trial of Allogeneic Cytomegalovirus-specific T Cells in Combination with Pembrolizumab for Recurrent Glioblastoma
papers.abstract: PurposeGlioblastoma (GBM) remains refractory to immunotherapy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment. Tumour-infiltrating cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells express elevated programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1), suggesting checkpoint-mediated dysfunction may limit T-cell therapy. We evaluated the safety and immunological activity of allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) combined with pembrolizumab. Patients and MethodsIn this phase I 3+3 dose-escalation study, recurrent GBM patients received four weekly infusions of CYT-101 followed by pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was safety. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival at 6 months (PFS-6), overall survival at 6 months (OS-6), and immune correlates of response. ResultsCYT-101 T-cell therapy demonstrated polyfunctional activity, broad HLA restriction, potent cytolytic function, and diverse T-cell receptor repertoires. Nine patients received study treatment. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Only six adverse events were considered treatment-related, and no treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity occurred. OS-6 and PFS-6 were 55% and 11%, respectively, with a median overall survival of 9.1 months. No objective clinical responses were seen. Of the nine treated participants, one had stable disease, five had progressive disease, and three were unevaluable by modified RANO criteria. Immune profiling revealed enhanced global CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function following CYT-101 therapy, while donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected in six of nine participants, with significant T-cell repertoire remodelling. ConclusionsAllogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy combined with pembrolizumab was safe in recurrent GBM, supporting further evaluation of this strategy to overcome immune dysfunction in GBM. Statement of Translational RelevanceGlioblastoma (GBM) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited benefit from immune checkpoint blockade or adoptive cellular therapies when used independently. This phase I study provides clinical evidence that combining an off-the-shelf, allogeneic cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) with PD-1 blockade is safe, feasible, and immunologically active in recurrent GBM. CYT-101 demonstrated a favourable safety profile without graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, or treatment-related serious adverse events. Importantly, donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected following infusion, accompanied by enhanced systemic CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function and substantial T-cell repertoire remodelling following CYT-101 and pembrolizumab. These findings provide proof-of-concept that allogeneic virus-specific T cells can be safely combined with checkpoint inhibition in GBM, supporting further clinical development and evaluation in larger studies.

papers.title: Hierarchical Graph Learning with Multimodal Distillation for Breast Cancer Survival Prediction
papers.abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and DNA methylation can provide complementary information for breast cancer prognosis, yet these measurements may be unavailable for new patients. In this paper, we propose HEAL-Surv, a teacher-student framework that uses both modalities during training to predict five-year net disease-specific survival (DSS) from clinical variables and molecular profiles at inference. An additive Cox teacher integrates all four modalities, using a hierarchical IMC graph encoder to capture local cell relationships and coarser tissue organisation. The student learns from observed outcomes and cross-fitted teacher survival curves, giving more weight to targets that agree across random initialisations. In five-fold cross-validation on 423 METABRIC patients, the full teacher achieved a mean five-year Unos concordance of 0.723. Removing any modality reduced mean concordance and increased mean Brier-based errors. Relative to the matched student trained on observed outcomes alone, distillation increased mean five-year Unos concordance from 0.658 to 0.704, with higher integrated and five-year Brier scores. In a separate external evaluation, an IMC-clinical variant trained on METABRIC achieved a five-year Unos concordance of 0.660 on 265 Basel patients without refitting. These findings support multimodal supervision for improving risk discrimination with fewer inference inputs, while external validation of the student remains necessary.

papers.title: Updated outcome of patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection enrolled in phase 2 clinical trials: A report from the Children's Oncology Group
papers.abstract: ObjectiveOsteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/MethodsThis study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. ResultsNinety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. ConclusionDespite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

papers.title: FlahyRecovery is an AI & gene expression based immune profiling biomarker for decision support in precision oncology
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccurate characterization of the tumor microenvironment (TME) is crucial for inferring tumor biology, subsequent tumor behavior, and predicting therapeutic response. Current characterization methods are inadequate in capturing the complexity of immune signaling networks, hindering robust clinical decision making. To address this, we have developed FlahyRecovery - an artificial intelligence (AI) and gene expression based immune profiling biomarker, implemented via a supervised classification machine learning model, that integrates response prediction and prognostic insights to personalize treatment design, particularly immunotherapy. MethodsGene expression data of 7424 tumor specimens across 14 cancers was annotated specimen wise into three immune subtypes: Elevated Immunity (Hot) with high cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, Suppressed Immunity (Cold) marked by immune exclusion and stromal dominance, and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) exhibiting mixed features. Following annotation validation, an AI model was trained and tested on the annotated data to classify new tumor specimens into the three immune subtypes - Elevated Immunity (Hot), Suppressed Immunity (Cold) and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) based on the expression of a panel of 1275 genes involved in immune cell signaling and immune signal transduction. ResultsIn a multi-tumor validation cohort (N=1337), the subtyping model showed a sensitivity of 79%, a specificity of 89%, and a one-vs-rest AUC of 0.93. Elevated Immunity tumors correlated with prolonged survival and immunotherapy response, while Suppressed Immunity tumors correlated with treatment resistance and need for combination therapy. ConclusionArtificial intelligence can be effectively used to process tumor biology digitized via next-generation sequencing, to accurately mark the TME from an immunological perspective. Its clinical utility mechanisms andying patients who can benefit from immunotherapies, identifying treatment resistance mechanisms, and informing combination treatment regimes.

papers.title: The LAMp-LC Study: Unveiling the lung microbiome in Australians with early- and late-stage lung cancer using shotgun metagenomics
papers.abstract: BackgroundLung cancer remains the leading cause of cancerl71related mortality, yet the role of lower airway microbiota in disease development and progression is incompletely defined. MethodsWe characterised the lung microbiome in an Australian cohort (lung cancer n=106, healthy n=10) using shotgun metagenomics and semil71quantitative culture to evaluate microbial ecology across the tumour microenvironment (TME), contralateral airways, and oral cavity, to evaluate microbiome differences across earlyl71 and latel71stage disease, and to quantify clinical covariate impacts on airway microbiota. Diversity analyses, multivariable linear modelling, and culturel71based comparisons were performed, with adjustment for smoking packl71years, sex, and tumour characteristics. ResultsCumulative smoking exposure caused significant, progressive Neisseria subflava, Gemella sanguinis, and Rothia mucilaginosa depletion, alongside Streptococcus mitis enrichment, with Mogibacterium diversum uniquely depleted within the TME of smokers. {beta} diversity in both early- and late-stage bronchial washes (BWs) significantly diverged from healthy controls, whilst diversity was significantly reduced in early-stage vs. late-stage BWs. The earlyl71stage TME demonstrated significantly reduced microbial cultivability compared with healthy and other lung cancer BWs. A small number of taxa were uniquely enriched (Sporothrix and Pseudomonas species) or depleted (Streptococcus parasanguinis, Streptococcus cristatus, R. mucilaginosa) within the TME, and 13 taxa were significantly enriched or depleted in both TME and contralateral airways compared with healthy airways. Only adenocarcinoma showed distinct oral {beta}l71diversity restructuring. ConclusionsThe lung cancer microbiome is characterised by early and progressive lower airway dysbiosis that is strongly shaped by tumour presence. Our findings point to potential new avenues for microbiomel71based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Detection of early-stage cancer using similarity-based classification of cell-free DNA fragmentation patterns
papers.abstract: Current cancer screening efforts face the dual problems of low patient adherence and a lack of available tests for many cancers, which motivates the development of less invasive multi-cancer early detection strategies. Such strategies will likely involve the use of liquid biopsies, which can analyze biomarkers found in blood for the presence of cancer. We introduce Blackjack, a new detection approach that focuses on the fragmentation patterns of plasma-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Blackjack characterizes a persons cfDNA fragmentation sites with a position probability matrix (PPM) that encodes information about the sequence context of the sites. For classification, Blackjack computes two features that represent the similarity of an individuals PPM to those of known healthy and cancer cohorts. With these two features, Blackjack then uses logistic regression to classify a new sample as being from a healthy individual or a person with cancer. In cross-validation experiments using two external whole genome sequencing datasets, Blackjack showed high performance, achieving a minimum area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.993 and minimum sensitivity (Sn) of 91.8% (at 98% specificity). This high performance was also present for stage I (AUC 0.991, Sn 89.8%) and stage II cancers (AUC 0.993, Sn 90.2%), and across eight different cancers (minimum AUC 0.985, minimum Sn 80.0%). We demonstrate that Blackjacks accuracy is stable at low simulated sequencing depths ([~]0.24x), and that tissue of origin prediction using Blackjacks similarity measures is high (minimum 82% accuracy of the top two predicted tissues). Our findings show that cfDNA fragmentation site contexts have valuable signals for early cancer detection, and that developing diagnostics with machine learning can benefit from a focus on having a small number of informative features.

papers.title: OVM-200, a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine, breaks immune tolerance to survivin in patients with advanced solid tumours: a multicentre, open-label, dose-expansion, phase 1 study
papers.abstract: Survivin (BIRC5) is broadly overexpressed in human cancers but, as a self-antigen, is subject to immune tolerance that limits spontaneous antitumour immunity. OVM-200 is a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine spanning full-length survivin, with cathepsin S-cleavable linker sequences inserted between adjacent peptides to enhance antigen processing and presentation. OVM-200-100 was a multicentre, open-label phase 1 study conducted at 4 UK sites. The pooled 2,000-g cohort comprised 27 patients with advanced non-small cell lung, ovarian or prostate cancer, including 24 patients from phase 1b and 3 treated at this dose in phase 1a. OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 3 initial vaccinations, with up to 8 additional doses in patients deriving clinical benefit. The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, secondary endpoints included survivin-specific immunogenicity, and antitumour activity by RECIST v1.1 was exploratory. OVM-200-related adverse events were exclusively grade 1-2, with no treatment-related grade [≥]3 adverse events, dose-limiting toxicities, serious adverse events or deaths. A systematic literature analysis showed low spontaneous anti-survivin seroreactivity in patients with cancer. In our cohort, pretreatment tumours expressed survivin despite low baseline survivin-specific immunity. OVM-200 vaccination subsequently induced robust humoral and cellular responses, with median anti-survivin IgG titres increasing from 20 at baseline to a peak of 81,920 and median interferon-{gamma} ELISpot responses increasing from 16.7 to 504.6 spot-forming units per 10 PBMCs. Patients receiving [≥]4 vaccinations developed higher anti-survivin antibody titres and stronger T cell responses than those receiving fewer doses. Among 24 RECIST-evaluable patients, the best overall response was stable disease (SD) in 6 patients (25%). Patients with SD had significantly higher anti-survivin antibody titres than those with progressive disease (PD) (p=0.0418). OVM-200 was well tolerated and induced robust survivin-specific immunity, providing clinical evidence that it can break immune tolerance to self-antigen survivin and supporting further development. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05104515.

papers.title: Quantitative evaluation of MGMT promoter methylation in FFPE and fresh frozen brain tumor samples by EpiDirect MGMT Methylation qPCR Assay compared to pyrosequencing: correlation and corresponding cutoffs
papers.abstract: MGMT promoter (MGMTp) methylation is a clinically important epigenetic biomarker that guides therapeutic decision-making in patients with glioblastoma and related brain malignancies. Pyrosequencing is a widely used method for analysis of MGMTp methylation in molecular pathology laboratories which relies on chemical conversion of DNA prior to amplification by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and subsequent sequencing. The EpiDirect(R) technology represents a novel analytical approach that enables direct, quantitative assessment of DNA methylation by qPCR using native, unmodified DNA. Here we compared the EpiDirect(R) MGMT Methylation qPCR Assay to MGMTp pyrosequencing using brain tumor samples to evaluate the correlation between the two methods. We show that there is a clear correlation across two different clinical cohorts involving both formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and fresh frozen samples and show that the EpiDirect(R) MGMT Methylation qPCR Assay is a valid alternative to pyrosequencing for quantitative assessment of MGMTp methylation in brain cancer samples.

papers.title: Regional Vulnerability to Brain Metastases Reflects Structural, Metabolic and Genetic Organization of the Healthy Brain
papers.abstract: BackgroundBrain metastases (BMs), the most common intracranial tumor, do not distribute uniformly throughout the brain, but instead preferentially localize to specific regions. Building on known associations with perfusion and the gray-white matter junction, we hypothesized that regional vulnerability to BMs also reflects the cellular and molecular organization of the healthy brain. MethodsIn a discovery cohort of 1,406 patients, we generated a voxelwise map of BM distribution and compared it with normative atlases of brain microstructure, vasculature, metabolism, cell-type composition, and gene expression. Associations were tested for replication in an independent multicenter validation cohort of 1,209 patients. ResultsIn the discovery cohort, BM frequency was higher near the gray-white matter junction and in regions with greater cerebral perfusion, glucose metabolism, and mitochondrial density. At the cellular level, BM frequency was inversely related to astrocyte and microglial transcriptional signatures. Using normative gene expression maps derived from postmortem healthy brain tissue, we identified 17 genes spatially associated with BM vulnerability and specific to metastases relative to other intracranial lesion types. These associations replicated in the validation cohort. The immune checkpoint gene LAG3 ranked among the ten genes most positively associated with metastatic vulnerability across all genes tested (r = 0.40-0.45, p < 0.001). LAG3 expression was also elevated in peritumoral brain metastasis tissue relative to control brain tissue in an independent spatial transcriptomic dataset. ConclusionsThese findings suggest that BM vulnerability reflects healthy brain organization and identify LAG-3, a clinically targetable immune checkpoint, as a candidate link between regional brain immune biology and metastatic colonization.

papers.title: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Like personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. ResultsAmong the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABAs unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancers output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABAs unfiltered output and Dellys output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABAs filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. ConclusionsAs all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

papers.title: The Complex Interplay Between Cancer and the Lung Microbiome
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe lung fosters a diverse microbiome that may have a complex interplay with underlying diseases, such as lung cancer. However, existing literature has revealed diverse results, likely owing to small sample sizes and diverse sampling methods. In this context, we aim to characterize the lung microbiome and its association with malignancy via multiple sampling methods during lung resection. MethodsPatients undergoing lung resection for confirmed malignancy were prospectively included in the study. During the operation, a bronchial swab and a parenchymal biopsy of lung tissue were collected from the resected specimen and sent for analysis via 16S rRNA gene amplicon (V4) sequencing. An established bioinformatics pipeline was used to determine taxonomic identification and compare these results to clinical and tumor data. ResultsThere were 83 participants included, with 75 (90.4%) patients having primary lung tumors and 8 (9.6%) having metastatic lesions. Resections included lobectomy (69.9%), wedge (25.3%), and segmentectomy (4.8%). Lung microbiome composition differed by primary malignancy site (lung vs metastatic; p=0.014) and tumor mutations (TP53, p=0.040; KRAS, p=0.054). For primary lung cancer, there was no difference in microbiome composition by tumor histology. A near-significant association was noted for patients with prolonged air leaks and alpha diversity of the lung microbiome (p=0.070). ConclusionsIn this study, we demonstrate associations between the lung microbiome and underlying malignancy and tumor characteristics. Validation of these results may assist with diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic interventions in the operative and peri-operative management of lung cancer.

papers.title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Incident Solid Cancers Resolved by Histologic Subtype: A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is a recognized precursor of myeloid malignancy and an independent cardiovascular risk factor, but its relationship with solid tumors is incompletely defined, particularly at histologic resolution. Here, we quantify the association between CHIP and incident cancer across hematologic and solid-organ sites, by clone size, mutation number, and histologic subtype in a prospective cohort of UK Biobank participants with baseline genetic sequencing and cancer ascertained by national registry linkage; those with pre-baseline cancer were excluded. Vanderbilt BioVU was used for replication. CHIP was associated with any incident cancer (HR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.18-1.27) and with all solid tumors combined (HR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.08-1.19). Among 17 endpoints, two survived multiple testing correction: lung adenocarcinoma (HR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.48-2.16) and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (HR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.37-3.81). Risk increased with clone size and multi-hit CHIP, most markedly for esophageal cancer (VAF [≥]30%: HR, 2.72), and the esophageal squamous association persisted in 5-year landmark analysis (HR, 2.57). In BioVU, CHIP was directionally associated with esophageal cancer and lung adenocarcinoma and its association with all solid tumors overall (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.17-1.32) was confirmed. These findings extend CHIP from a hematologic and cardiovascular risk marker to a risk marker of solid-organ cancer risk with histologic resolution and motivate clone-size-aware risk models and mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
papers.abstract: BackgroundLow-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. MethodsWe analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I-III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. ResultsThe multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67-0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64-0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71-0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62-1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage-GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. ConclusionsMulti-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.
